name: ECG 5 · Ischaemia
blurb: Spot a STEMI, locate the artery and unmask its mimics.

topics.name: Reading the ST segment
topics.desc: Where the ST starts, what baseline to use, which shapes worry you.

cards.q: Explain: The J point starts the ST
cards.a: The ST segment runs from the end of the QRS to the upstroke of the T wave. The point where it leaves the QRS is the J point (junction point).
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.107; Thaler ch6 p.248

cards.q:
Acute MI is diagnosed early from the ST segment, not from Q waves or enzymes.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Reperfusion must start within hours, long before Q waves form or enzymes come back.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.107

cards.q: Why does Thaler prefer the TP segment as the baseline?
cards.a:
Pericarditis can depress the PR segment

A depressed PR segment makes the ST look falsely elevated, so the TP segment is safer.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.247; Khan ch5 p.107

cards.q: Name every lead with ST elevation
cards.a:
II, III, aVF

II, III and aVF are raised well above 1 mm; I and aVL are depressed.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.109; Thaler ch6 p.249

cards.q: Explain: Concave is usually benign
cards.a: A concave ST segment (scooped upward, like a smile) with a separate T wave is typical of the normal variant. Khan describes a notched J point and a "fishhook" shape.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.110, p.123; Thaler ch6 p.248

cards.q: Which ST shape most suggests acute myocardial injury?
cards.a:
Convex, merging into the T wave

Injury current domes the ST so it fuses with the T wave.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.248; Khan ch5 p.110

cards.q: Match each finding to what it means
cards.a:
ST depression: Ischaemia
ST elevation: Injury current
Pathological Q wave: Necrosis

Khan's classic triad: ischaemia, injury, infarction.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.241; Khan ch5 p.109

cards.q: Which ST depression is the weakest sign of ischaemia?
cards.a:
Upsloping, 1.5 mm

Upsloping depression gives many false positives; horizontal and downsloping are the significant types.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.129; Thaler ch6 p.284

cards.q:
A 0.5 mm ST depression in an asymptomatic patient is diagnostic of ischaemia.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Depression ≤ 1 mm without typical symptoms is nonspecific.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.129

cards.q: ST elevation in aVR greater than in V1 suggests occlusion of the
cards.a:
Left main coronary artery

Khan gives aVR elevation exceeding V1 as a marker of left main obstruction.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.120

topics.name: STEMI, step by step
topics.desc: How an occluded artery evolves on the ECG, and the criteria.

cards.q: A man gets chest tightness after two flights of stairs, gone after 3 minutes of rest, unchanged for a year. This is
cards.a:
Stable angina

Pain at a fixed level of exertion, relieved by rest, with a stable pattern is stable angina.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.240

cards.q: A thrombus totally occludes a coronary artery. The expected ECG syndrome is
cards.a:
STEMI

Complete occlusion causes transmural injury and ST elevation.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.240–241

cards.q: Explain: First sign: the hyperacute T
cards.a: Minutes into an infarct the T waves grow tall and peaked, nearly equalling or exceeding the QRS in the same lead. These are hyperacute T waves. Get serial ECGs minutes apart if the first is not diagnostic.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.245–246; Khan ch8 p.206

cards.q: Name every lead with ST elevation
cards.a:
V1, V2, V3, V4

V1–V4 are raised; the inferior leads show reciprocal depression.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.247; Khan ch5 p.109

cards.q: Put the acute STEMI changes in their usual order
cards.a:
Hyperacute T wave → ST elevation → Q wave → T-wave inversion

Peaked T first, then injury, then necrosis; the T inverts as the ST settles.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.118, ch6 p.146–147; Thaler ch6 p.250

cards.q: Name the leads with reciprocal ST depression
cards.a:
I, aVL

An inferior STEMI is mirrored in the high lateral leads I and aVL.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.251; Khan ch5 p.118

cards.q: A 55-year-old man: how many mm of ST elevation in V2 must be exceeded?
cards.a:
2 mm

Men over 40 need more than 2.0 mm in V2–V3.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.249

cards.q: Which pair is contiguous?
cards.a:
III and aVF

III and aVF both look at the inferior wall.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.249, p.253; Khan ch5 p.109

cards.q: Chest pain for 1 hour, ST elevation in II, III, aVF. The next step is
cards.a:
Immediate reperfusion, ideally PCI

A STEMI with a consistent history goes straight to reperfusion; enzymes are not awaited.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.243, p.252; Khan ch5 p.120

cards.q: Which finding usually lasts for life after a STEMI?
cards.a:
Pathological Q waves

Q waves of necrosis usually persist; the ST settles within hours to days.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246, p.252; Khan ch6 p.152

topics.name: Where is the infarct?
topics.desc: Map the leads to the wall and the wall to the artery.

cards.q: An inferior STEMI with complete heart block. Which artery supplies both regions in most people?
cards.a:
Right coronary

The RCA supplies the inferior wall and usually the AV node.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.253

cards.q: Name the leads that show the inferior infarct
cards.a:
II, III, aVF

II, III and aVF face the diaphragmatic surface.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.254; Khan ch6 p.157

cards.q: Explain: Anterior: V1–V4, the LAD
cards.a: An anterior infarct shows in the chest leads, typically V1–V4, from the LAD. Khan: V1–V3 alone was called anteroseptal, but most such infarcts are really anteroapical. Reciprocal change appears inferiorly.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.256; Khan ch5 p.111, ch6 p.158

cards.q: Name every lead with ST elevation
cards.a:
I, aVL, V5, V6

The four lateral leads are elevated; III and aVF are reciprocally depressed.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.255; Khan ch6 p.158

cards.q: Explain: Posterior: read V1–V3 as a mirror
cards.a: No standard lead faces the posterior wall, so look for its mirror image in V1–V3: ST depression and a tall R wave (R > S in V1), usually with an upright T.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.258; Khan ch6 p.161–162

cards.q: Which leads show a posterior STEMI as ST elevation?
cards.a:
V7–V9

V7–V9 sit on the back over the posterior wall.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.259; Khan ch6 p.162

cards.q: Explain: Inferoposterior and anterolateral combinations
cards.a: Posterior infarcts rarely occur alone: expect inferior ST elevation plus ST depression and tall R in V1–V3 (inferoposterior). Chest-lead elevation plus I and aVL is anterolateral; Thaler links it to left main occlusion.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.258, p.262; Khan ch6 p.158

cards.q: In an inferior STEMI, which finding suggests right ventricular involvement?
cards.a:
ST elevation in V4R

ST elevation in V3R–V4R is the diagnostic sign of RV infarction.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.260; Khan ch5 p.111, ch6 p.158

cards.q:
Sublingual nitroglycerin is safe in an inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R.
True or false?
cards.a: False. RV infarction is preload sensitive; nitrates can cause severe hypotension.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.261; Khan ch5 p.111

cards.q: Match each lead group to its usual artery
cards.a:
II, III, aVF: Right coronary
V1–V4: LAD
I, aVL, V5, V6: Circumflex
Tall R and ST depression V1–V3: Right coronary (posterior)

Lead groups face walls; each wall has a usual artery.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.253–254; Khan ch6 p.157

topics.name: NSTEMI and angina
topics.desc: Ischaemia without ST elevation, and the patterns that hide an LAD.

cards.q: Chest pain, raised troponin, 2 mm ST depression in V3–V5, no elevation. Diagnosis?
cards.a:
NSTEMI

ST depression with a raised troponin and no elevation is an NSTEMI.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.263; Khan ch5 p.127

cards.q:
An NSTEMI is a transmural infarct that leaves deep Q waves.
True or false?
cards.a: False. It is subendocardial and does not evolve deep Q waves.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.263; Khan ch5 p.127

cards.q: Rest pain, ST depression in V4–V6, troponin normal on serial testing. Diagnosis?
cards.a:
Unstable angina

Same ECG as NSTEMI, but no troponin rise, so no infarction.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.242, p.265; Khan ch5 p.129

cards.q:
A normal ECG between attacks rules out unstable angina.
True or false?
cards.a: False. The ECG is usually normal between attacks; changes appear during pain.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.241, p.265

cards.q: Explain: Wellens: deep T inversion V2–V3
cards.a: Wellens' syndrome: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 (sometimes V4), often recorded when the patient is pain-free. It predicts a critical proximal LAD stenosis and impending anterior MI.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.257; Khan ch5 p.133

cards.q: Explain: Biphasic Wellens: up, then down
cards.a: The biphasic form of Wellens' has the upright part first, then a terminally inverted part. Khan notes a "hitched-up" ST before the deep inversion. Do not stress-test these patients; they need angiography.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.257; Khan ch5 p.129, p.133

cards.q: Explain: De Winter: an LAD occlusion without elevation
cards.a: De Winter T waves: upsloping ST depression at the J point running into tall, symmetric T waves across the chest leads. About 2 % of acute LAD occlusions look like this. Treat it as a STEMI.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.257

cards.q: ST elevation at rest that resolves fully after nitroglycerin, normal troponin. Most likely
cards.a:
Prinzmetal angina

Coronary spasm gives transient ST elevation that settles with nitrates.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.266; Khan ch5 p.124

cards.q: Which exercise test finding is positive for coronary disease?
cards.a:
Horizontal 1.5 mm depression for 0.08 s after J

Horizontal or downsloping depression over 1 mm, lasting 0.08 s past J, is positive.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.284

cards.q: Match each syndrome to its ST change and troponin
cards.a:
STEMI: ST elevation, troponin up
NSTEMI: ST depression, troponin up
Unstable angina: ST depression, troponin normal
Prinzmetal angina: ST elevation, troponin normal

ST direction plus troponin separates all four.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.267

topics.name: Q waves
topics.desc: Tell the scar of an old infarct from a normal q.

cards.q: Why does an electrode over an old infarct record a Q wave?
cards.a:
Forces move away from the silent scar

With the scar silent, the net current flows away from that electrode.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.250

cards.q: Where are small septal q waves normally found?
cards.a:
I, aVL, V5 and V6

Left-to-right septal depolarisation moves away from the left lateral leads.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.251; Khan ch6 p.141

cards.q: Which Q wave is pathological by Thaler's criteria?
cards.a:
0.04 s, 40 % of the R

It is at least 0.04 s wide and over 25 % of the R height.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.251; Khan ch6 p.137

cards.q:
A Q wave in lead III alone, with none in II or aVF, means an old inferior MI.
True or false?
cards.a: False. An isolated Q in III is a common normal variant.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.252; Khan ch6 p.147, p.152

cards.q: Which lead should never be used to diagnose infarction from Q waves?
cards.a:
aVR

aVR faces the cavity of the heart and normally records a deep Q or QS.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.251; Khan ch6 p.137

cards.q: Match each lead to its normal Q limit (Khan)
cards.a:
Lead I: ≤ 1.5 mm deep
II and aVF: ≤ 0.03 s, < 4 mm
Lead III: ≤ 0.04 s, < 10 mm
V5 and V6: ≤ 0.03 s, < 3 mm

Khan sets lead-specific limits; III tolerates the widest and deepest Q.
cards.note: Khan ch6 p.139–141

cards.q: A QS in V2 on a routine ECG of a well patient. First step?
cards.a:
Repeat with correct lead placement

V1–V2 placed too high is a common cause of a false QS.
cards.note: Khan ch6 p.157–158; Thaler ch6 p.290

cards.q: Q waves in II, III, aVF with an isoelectric ST and inverted T. The infarct is
cards.a:
Old or age indeterminate

Q waves with a settled ST point to an established, older infarct.
cards.note: Khan ch6 p.152, p.157; Thaler ch6 p.252

cards.q: Q-like waves in II, III, aVF with a short PR interval. Most likely cause?
cards.a:
Wolff–Parkinson–White

Negative delta waves mimic inferior Q waves; the short PR gives WPW away.
cards.note: Khan ch6 p.163–168; Thaler ch6 p.283

cards.q:
Poor R wave progression is specific for anterior infarction.
True or false?
cards.a: False. LVH, LBBB, COPD, obesity and lead misplacement cause it too.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.256; Khan ch6 p.142–146

topics.name: T wave abnormalities
topics.desc: Normal T, peaked T, flipped T, and how to report them.

cards.q: In which lead is an inverted T wave always normal?
cards.a:
aVR

aVR looks at the heart from the right shoulder, so all its waves are negative.
cards.note: Khan ch8 p.194–195

cards.q: Explain: Normal T: asymmetric and modest
cards.a: A normal T rises slowly and falls faster: it is asymmetric. Khan: usually < 5 mm in limb leads and < 10 mm in chest leads, and at least 0.5 mm in I and II.
cards.note: Khan ch8 p.206, ch5 p.129; Thaler ch6 p.246

cards.q: Which is NOT a cause of tall T waves in Khan's list?
cards.a:
Hypokalaemia

Hypokalaemia flattens T waves and brings U waves; the others make T waves tall.
cards.note: Khan ch8 p.206

cards.q:
T inversion in V4 with 1.5 mm horizontal ST depression supports ischaemia.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Khan: T inversion with horizontal ST depression > 1 mm allows a confident ischaemia diagnosis.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246; Khan ch8 p.198

cards.q: A slow downslope and quick upslope T inversion in V6 with huge voltages most suggests
cards.a:
LVH with strain

Asymmetric inversion with high voltage is the secondary repolarisation change of LVH.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246

cards.q: Comatose patient, giant wide T inversion and a long QT across the chest leads. Think of
cards.a:
Subarachnoid haemorrhage

Deep, broad T inversion with QT prolongation is the classic CNS pattern.
cards.note: Khan ch8 p.200–205

cards.q:
T inversion in V1–V3 in a healthy 19-year-old can be normal.
True or false?
cards.a: True. The persistent juvenile T pattern inverts V1–V3 in some young adults.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246; Khan ch8 p.202

cards.q: Previously inverted T waves become upright during chest pain. This is
cards.a:
Pseudonormalisation

Ischaemia can flip inverted T waves upright; only comparison reveals it.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.246

cards.q: Flat T waves in V4–V6 with 0.5 mm ST depression, no symptoms. Best report?
cards.a:
Nonspecific ST-T changes; ischaemia not excluded

Minor ST-T changes are nonspecific, but ischaemia must stay on the list.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.129, ch8 p.199

cards.q:
Isolated T-wave inversion is diagnostic of myocardial infarction.
True or false?
cards.a: False. T inversion has many causes; on its own it is nonspecific.
cards.note: Khan ch8 p.199–202; Thaler ch6 p.246

topics.name: STEMI mimics
topics.desc: ST elevation that is not an occluded artery, and how to tell.

cards.q: Explain: Pericarditis: diffuse and concave
cards.a: Acute pericarditis raises the ST in many leads at once, not confined to one artery's territory. The ST stays concave (saddle shaped) and Q waves never form.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.303; Khan ch5 p.124, ch10 p.225

cards.q: Name every lead with ST depression
cards.a:
aVR

In pericarditis only aVR (and sometimes V1) shows ST depression.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.225; Thaler ch7 p.303

cards.q: Order the stages of acute pericarditis
cards.a:
Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression → ST and PR return to baseline → Diffuse T-wave inversion → T waves normalise

In pericarditis the T inverts only after the ST has settled.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.225; Thaler ch7 p.303

cards.q: Explain: Early repolarisation: young and fishhooked
cards.a: Benign early repolarisation: concave ST elevation of 1 to 4 mm, mostly V2–V5, with a notched J point (fishhook), in young people. No reciprocal depression. Unlike ischaemia, it does not grow over 15 to 60 minutes of serial ECGs.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.123; Thaler ch6 p.248–249

cards.q: Explain: LVH can raise V1–V3
cards.a: LVH (criteria in level 4) gives deep S waves and sometimes ST elevation in V1–V3, plus lateral strain depression. Khan: LVH can also cause poor R progression and QS in V1–V3, mimicking an anteroseptal MI.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.126, ch6 p.168

cards.q:
Discordant ST elevation in V1–V3 with an old LBBB is by itself diagnostic of STEMI.
True or false?
cards.a: False. LBBB normally produces discordant ST elevation in the right chest leads.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.126; Thaler ch6 p.282

cards.q: Name every lead with concordant ST elevation
cards.a:
I, aVL, V5, V6

In these leads the QRS is upright and the ST rises with it: concordant.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.282; Khan ch6 p.174–175

cards.q: How is takotsubo cardiomyopathy distinguished from a STEMI?
cards.a:
Normal coronary angiogram

The ECG cannot separate them; the cath lab shows no occluded artery.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.264

cards.q: Anterior Q waves and 2 mm ST elevation in V2–V4, unchanged since an MI 5 months ago. Most likely
cards.a:
Left ventricular aneurysm

ST elevation persisting over 4 weeks with old Q waves points to an aneurysm.
cards.note: Khan ch5 p.124, p.127, ch6 p.157; Thaler ch6 p.248

cards.q: Explain: Two more mimics for level 6
cards.a: Two more ST mimics come in level 6: - Brugada pattern: coved ST elevation in V1–V2 - Hyperkalaemia: peaked T waves, sometimes ST elevation For now, recognise the names.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.268
